figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Sources of supervision for post-training in end-to-end autonomous driving. (a) Environment-derived rewards from closed-loop interaction with a simulator or world model. (b) Trajectory scores from an external rule-based or learned scorer. (c) NegWAM uses offline-mined negative trajectories as repulsive anchors and scene-conditioned rider tokens to introduce negative-aware losses into a unified world–action model.
figures.headline: NegWAM's supervision comes from offline-mined negative trajectories, not from closed-loop environments or external trajectory scorers.
citing_sentences: One line of work (Figure 1a) explores policies in closed-loop environments built with a simulator [9, 10] or a world model [11, 12], but is constrained by the sim-to-real gap, environment construction costs, and reconstruction artifacts [13, 12].

Another line (Figure 1b) scores candidate trajectories using rule-based evaluators or learned reward models, but the quality of its supervision is limited by handcrafted rules, privileged information, and evaluator bias [14, 15, 16].
Building on this insight, we propose NegWAM, a negative-aware safety post-training method that incorporates offline negative supervision into a unified WAM (Figure 1c).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Architecture of our NegWAM. In Stage 1, we adapt a pretrained world-action DiT into a unified world–action model through flow matching. In Stage 2, scene-specific hard-negative trajectories are used as both repulsive anchors and trajectory riders for compatibility learning. The auxiliary rider branch is removed at inference, introducing no additional deployment cost.
figures.headline: NegWAM keeps the stage-one flow-matching backbone and adds repulsive anchors and rider tokens that are removed at inference.
citing_sentences: Figure 2 illustrates how repulsive anchors and scene-conditioned rider tokens introduce these signals into the same backbone while retaining its flow-matching objective.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Scene-conditioned rider tokens for scene–trajectory compatibility learning. Expert and negative riders attend to observed scene tokens through shared DiT attention, and their compatibility scores define a ranking loss that updates the shared backbone.
figures.headline: Expert and negative rider tokens attend to observed scene tokens, and their scores drive a ranking loss that updates the shared backbone.
citing_sentences: Figure 3 illustrates the shared attention and scoring pathway.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Scene–trajectory compatibility scores for three example scenes. Rows correspond to the trajectories shown on the left, and columns correspond to the observed scenes shown above. Each cell reports the compatibility score of the corresponding scene–trajectory pair.
figures.headline: Compatibility scores vary across three scenes, and mismatched scene-trajectory pairs receive negative scores.
citing_sentences: Figure 4 further illustrates the scene–trajectory compatibility learned by the rider branch.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Effect of Post-Training Steps for NAVSIM v2 navhard. NegWAM results are reported as mean $\pm$ one standard deviation over three random seeds, while the baseline is a single run.
figures.headline: On navhard, NegWAM outperforms the standard post-training baseline at every budget from 10K to 30K steps, averaged over three seeds.
citing_sentences: As shown in Figure 5, NegWAM consistently outperforms the matched standard post-training baseline from 10K to 30K steps, confirming that the improvement holds across the post-training budget rather than at a single checkpoint.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Effect of Post-Training Steps for NAVSIMv2 navtest. NegWAM results are reported as mean $\pm$ one standard deviation over three random seeds, while the baseline is a single run.
figures.headline: On navtest, NegWAM shows consistent gains over the baseline from 5K to 30K post-training steps.
citing_sentences: The corresponding navtest results in Figure 6 also show consistent gains over the baseline from 5K to 30K steps.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Qualitative comparison between DriveWAM [7] and our NegWAM in safety-critical scenarios. DriveWAM (top) predicts trajectories that approach nearby traffic participants, whereas NegWAM (bottom) maintains safer clearance while better following the human-expert trajectory.
figures.headline: In safety-critical scenes, NegWAM keeps greater clearance from nearby traffic than DriveWAM while still following the expert trajectory.
citing_sentences: As shown in Figure 7, NegWAM maintains safer clearance than DriveWAM [7] and avoids potential collision regions.

figures.caption: Representative closed-loop rollout in HUGSIM. Rows are ordered chronologically from top to bottom, with three rendered camera views at each time point. Yellow dots mark the overlaid trajectory in the center view. An oncoming vehicle approaches and passes on the left as the ego vehicle proceeds along the road.
figures.headline: A representative HUGSIM closed-loop rollout shows an oncoming vehicle passing on the left as the ego vehicle proceeds along the road.
citing_sentences: Figure 8 shows a representative closed-loop rollout in HUGSIM.

figures.caption: Additional closed-loop rollout near a junction in HUGSIM. The four rows are ordered chronologically from top to bottom; each row contains three rendered camera views. Yellow dots show the overlaid trajectory in the center view. A nearby white vehicle is visible in the early snapshots, followed by the ego vehicle’s continued motion along the road.
figures.headline: An additional HUGSIM rollout near a junction shows a white vehicle leaving the views as the ego vehicle advances.
citing_sentences: Figure 9 shows an additional closed-loop interaction in HUGSIM [21].

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Additional successful cases. Comparison between DriveWAM [7] (top) and NegWAM (bottom) in an intersection-straight scenario with a stopped roadside vehicle and an intersection left-turn scenario. NegWAM safely avoids the stopped vehicle and maintains its trajectory within the drivable area, while the baseline produces collision-prone or off-road trajectories.
figures.headline: NegWAM avoids a stopped roadside vehicle and stays on the drivable area in an intersection left turn, where DriveWAM does not.
citing_sentences: Figure 10 compares DriveWAM with NegWAM in two scenarios beyond those shown in the main paper.

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Representative failure cases. Comparison between DriveWAM (top) and NegWAM (bottom). In the first case, NegWAM fails to follow the expert’s leftward overtaking maneuver and collides with the stopped leading vehicle, whereas DriveWAM avoids the collision through conservative deceleration. In the second case, NegWAM maintains insufficient clearance from a vehicle in the target lane while turning, resulting in a collision.
figures.headline: Two failure cases show NegWAM colliding with a stopped leading vehicle during an overtake and turning with insufficient clearance, where DriveWAM avoids collision.
citing_sentences: Figure 11 documents two cases in which NegWAM performs worse than DriveWAM.

abstract: World-action models (WAMs) jointly model future traffic states and driving actions for end-to-end autonomous driving in intelligent transportation systems. However, their action learning remains dominated by expert-trajectory imitation, leaving unsafe alternatives close to expert trajectories insufficiently constrained. To improve WAM robustness in safety-critical scenarios, we propose NegWAM, a safety post-training framework for unified WAMs that learns explicit safety boundaries from near-expert failure trajectories. NegWAM constructs negative trajectories that are geometrically close to the expert trajectory yet carry safety risks, uses them as repulsive anchors to steer predictions away from dangerous behavior, and encodes them as scene-conditioned rider tokens to learn scene–trajectory compatibility. During training, NegWAM jointly optimizes the flow-matching and near-expert negative objectives, while the auxiliary rider branch is discarded at inference, incurring no additional overhead. On NAVSIM v2, NegWAM achieves 40.4 EPDMS on navhard, a 4.1 % relative improvement over the strongest compared scorer-free WAM baseline, and achieves 93.3 EPDMS on navtest. These results demonstrate that NegWAM achieves strong performance in safety-critical scenarios while preserving routine-driving performance. Zero-shot closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM further demonstrates cross-benchmark generalization. The code is available at https://github.com/Zizizi-hao/NegWAM.

sections.body: The introduction argues that flow-matching imitation of expert trajectories does not tell a world-action model which near-expert alternatives to reject. Existing post-training uses simulator or world-model rollouts, or external trajectory scorers, each with limits the paper states. NegWAM instead mines near-expert negative trajectories offline and uses them as repulsive anchors and scene-conditioned rider tokens. The rider branch is removed at inference. On NAVSIM v2, NegWAM reports 40.4 EPDMS on navhard, a 4.1 % relative improvement over the strongest compared scorer-free WAM baseline, and 93.3 EPDMS on navtest, against a strongest baseline score of 92.9. Zero-shot HUGSIM evaluation gives an HD-Score of 30.6 against 27.2 for DriveWAM.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: World-action models learn only from expert trajectories, leaving nearby unsafe alternatives unconstrained, which motivates safety post-training.

sections.body: This section reviews end-to-end driving, world-action models, and driving post-training. Expert demonstrations contain few safety-critical failures, and geometric similarity to an expert trajectory does not establish that an action is safe. Shared video-action transformers trained with flow matching fit demonstrated video-action sequences without explicitly contrasting expert trajectories against undesirable alternatives. Other post-training methods use simulated rollouts, learned rewards, or preference pairs. DriveDPO and BeyondDrive use near-expert unsafe trajectories, with distinct policy objectives and negative constructions. The review positions NegWAM as learning both repulsion and scene compatibility from the same offline-mined failures, while keeping the flow-matching objective active throughout post-training.
sections.heading: Literature Review
sections.headline: Prior work shows near-expert failures are useful supervision, but unified world-action models do not explicitly contrast expert trajectories with them.

sections.body: NegWAM starts from a shared checkpoint of a unified world-action model built on Wan2.2-TI2V-5B and adds a second post-training stage. Negatives come from the 16K dense GTRS trajectory vocabulary, because sampling from the current policy gave an average pairwise ADE of only 0.02 m across eight trajectories for one scene. Candidates with ADE below 1.0 m are kept if their 40-step trajectories score zero EPDMS. At each iteration they are subsampled to eight steps, filtered to the range [0.3,1.0) m, and at most K=16 are sampled. At least one valid hard negative exists for 85.8 % of training samples. Repulsion uses a distance-adaptive margin with alpha=0.9, and the compatibility ranking loss uses temperature 0.1. Rider groups and the compatibility head are discarded at inference.
sections.heading: Methods
sections.headline: Near-expert failures mined offline supply repulsive anchor and scene-compatibility losses added to flow-matching post-training.

sections.body: Table I reports navhard results under the corrected NAVSIM v2.2 protocol, with NegWAM at 40.4 EPDMS, above BeyondDrive at 38.8 and DriveWAM at 37.7. Table VIII reports navtest, where NegWAM scores 93.3 against 92.9 for BeyondDrive, with DAC at 98.4 against 97.7. Zero-shot HUGSIM closed-loop evaluation gives an HD-Score of 30.6 against 27.2 for DriveWAM. Inference latency rises from 871.35 ms to 877.86 ms, a difference of 6.51 ms (0.75 %), with the same model size and peak GPU memory. Across the tested hyperparameter settings in Table V, EPDMS ranges from 39.0 to 40.4.
sections.heading: Experiments and Results
sections.headline: NegWAM reaches 40.4 EPDMS on navhard and 93.3 on navtest, a 4.1 % relative gain over the strongest scorer-free baseline.

sections.body: The conclusion restates that NegWAM uses offline-constructed near-expert hard negatives as repulsive anchors and scene-conditioned rider tokens. The authors report improved performance in challenging scenarios with routine driving performance preserved. They state that post-training needs no online simulation and adds no inference overhead. Zero-shot HUGSIM evaluation is cited as evidence that the learned boundaries transfer to unseen interactive environments. The stated limitation is that generalization to the diversity and unpredictability of real-world driving remains to be established. Future work is named as more generalizable and adaptive safety learning for world-action models, combined with long-horizon decision-making.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: NegWAM adds no inference overhead, but its generalization to diverse real-world driving remains to be established.

sections.body:
- Table VII lists model size (6,241.81 MB) and peak GPU memory (14,029.08 MB), pretraining for 100K steps (22 h, 88 GPU hours), and safety post-training for 10K steps (2 h, 8 GPU hours).
- The scheduler and negative-cache sections give the shifted noise scales and the eight-step pose indexing used for training trajectories.
- Table VIII gives full navtest component scores, with NegWAM at 93.3 EPDMS.
- Figures 9 to 11 show an additional HUGSIM junction rollout, further trajectory comparisons, and failure cases where NegWAM collides and DriveWAM does not.
- The scope section states that rare maneuvers outside the vocabulary receive no negative supervision, that the zero-EPDMS label inherits evaluator assumptions, and that the evidence gives no formal safety guarantee.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers training configuration, full navtest component scores, additional qualitative cases, failure cases, and limits of the negative supervision.
